entry: Island group lying north of the Canadian mainland, in the [[Arctic Ocean]]. Also known as the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, it excludes [[Greenland]] and [[Iceland]] and covers about 1,424,500 sq km (550,000 sq mi). Its 36,563 islands include 94 major islands, and much of the group lies in [[Nunavut]] and the [[Northwest Territories]]. Only 11 islands are populated; [[Baffin Island]], the largest, has the largest population, 13,309. Paleo-Eskimos arrived about 2500 BCE, and the Thule people, ancestors of today's [[Inuit]], replaced them between 1000 and 1500 CE. Britain transferred the islands to Canada by 1880. Canada claims the waterways of the [[Northwest Passage]] as internal waters, but most maritime countries consider them international waters.

Northernmost of the five major circles of latitude, and one of the two polar circles. Its southern counterpart is the [[Antarctic Circle]]. The circle lies at about 66° 34′ N and currently at 66°33′51.1″ N, a latitude that depends on [[Axial tilt|Earth's axial tilt]], which fluctuates by some 2° over a 41,000-year period. It is the southernmost latitude at which the Sun does not rise on the December solstice or does not set on the June solstice, phenomena called [[Polar night|polar night]] and [[Midnight sun|midnight sun]]. In [[Murmansk]], three degrees north of the circle, the Sun stays below the horizon for 20 days before and after the [[Winter solstice|winter solstice]], and above it for 20 days before and after the [[Summer solstice|summer solstice]]. The circle drifts toward the North Pole by about 14.5 m (48 ft) per year.

English rock band, formed in [[Sheffield]] in 2002. Its debut album, *Whatever People Say I Am, That's What I'm Not* (2006), topped the UK Albums Chart and was then the fastest-selling debut album in British chart history. The band was among the first to reach public attention via the Internet, during the "blog rock" era. Its fifth album, *AM* (2013), brought wider international fame, with the single "Do I Wanna Know?". The band has won seven Brit Awards and a Mercury Prize, and has been nominated for nine [[Grammy Awards]].

Small fox native to the Arctic regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]], common across the [[Tundra|Arctic tundra]]. The species, *Vulpes lagopus*, has thick fur that camouflages it against snow in winter and provides the best insulation of any mammal. Its coat has two genetically distinct color morphs, white and blue; the white morph makes up about 90% of the global population. The Arctic fox eats [[Lemming|lemmings]], [[Vole|voles]], ringed seal pups, fish and [[Seabird|seabirds]], as well as carrion and berries. Breeding pairs are monogamous and raise their young in complex underground dens. Natural predators include [[Golden eagle|golden eagles]], [[Polar bear|polar bears]] and [[Wolverine|wolverines]].

Extinct genus of short-faced bears that inhabited North America during the [[Pleistocene]]. Two species are recognized: the lesser short-faced bear (*Arctodus pristinus*) and the giant short-faced bear (*Arctodus simus*). The larger *A. simus* is among the best-known members of North America's Ice Age [[Megafauna|megafauna]] and is believed to be one of the largest terrestrial [[Carnivora|carnivorans]] ever to have existed. Adult *A. simus* ranged between 300–950 kg (660–2,090 lb), with males around 800 kg (1,800 lb). It disappeared about 12,800 years ago, in the [[Late Pleistocene extinctions]].

Red giant star, and the brightest star in the northern constellation Boötes. Its Bayer designation is α Boötis. With an [[Apparent magnitude|apparent visual magnitude]] of −0.05, it is the fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere. It lies 36.7 light-years from the [[Sun]] and is a red giant of spectral type K1.5III, about 7.1 billion years old, that has used up its core hydrogen and left the [[Main sequence|main sequence]]. It has about the same mass as the Sun but has expanded to 25 times its size, around 35 million kilometers, and is about 170 times as luminous. Its name is Latinized from the [[Ancient Greek|ancient Greek]] and means "Guardian of the Bear."

Palm family of perennial [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the [[Monocotyledon|monocot]] order Arecales. Its members include climbers, [[Shrub|shrubs]], stemless plants and tree-like palms. The family comprises 181 [[Genus|genera]] with around 2,600 [[Species|species]], most restricted to tropical and subtropical climates. Most palms have large, compound, evergreen leaves called fronds, arranged at the top of an unbranched stem; the genus Hyphaene is an exception, with branched palms. Palms inhabit nearly every type of habitat, from [[Rainforest|rainforests]] to [[Desert|deserts]]. They are among the best-known and most extensively cultivated plant families, and a wide range of common products and foods are derived from them. In many historical cultures, palms were symbols of victory, peace and fertility.

City in southern [[Peru]], capital of Arequipa Province (pop., 2025 projected: 1,195,700). It is the country's second most populous city after [[Lima]] and the official seat of the Constitutional Court of Peru, and is known as the "Legal Capital of Peru." The city was founded on August 15, 1540, on both banks of the Chili River, in a valley bordered by the [[Andes]]. Its industries include manufactured goods, textiles made from camelid [[Wool|wool]], and the production of copper and [[Molybdenum|molybdenum]] concentrates. In the 19th and 20th centuries it acted as a counterweight to centralized power in Lima. In 2000, [[UNESCO]] inscribed 332 hectares of its historic center as a [[World Heritage Site]].

Greek god of war and courage, one of the [[Twelve Olympians|Twelve Olympians]]. Son of [[Zeus]] and [[Hera]], he embodied the physical valor needed for success in war, but also brutality and bloodlust, in contrast to his sister [[Athena]]. Many Greeks were ambivalent toward him, and he has a limited role in Greek mythology, where he is often humiliated. In the [[Trojan War]], [[Aphrodite]] persuaded him to side with the Trojans, and [[Hephaestus]] trapped him and Aphrodite in a net. His nearest Roman counterpart is [[Mars]].

American singer-songwriter and pianist, known as the "Queen of Soul." Franklin began singing gospel at New Bethel Baptist Church in [[Detroit]], Michigan, where her father, C. L. Franklin, was a minister. She was signed by [[Columbia Records]] at 18, but her career did not immediately flourish. After she joined Atlantic Records in 1966, she recorded hits including *I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You* and *Lady Soul*. Her rendition of "Respect" is often called her signature song. After she joined Arista Records in 1979, *Jump to It* and *Who's Zoomin' Who?* revived her career. She has sold more than 75 million records worldwide and won 18 [[Grammy Awards]] out of 44 nominations. In 1987 she became the first female artist inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. In 2019 the [[Pulitzer Prize]] jury gave her a posthumous special citation for her "indelible contribution to American music and culture for more than five decades."

Men's [[Association football|association football]] team representing [[Argentina]]. It has been a member of [[FIFA]] since 1912 and has won three [[FIFA World Cup|FIFA World Cups]], in 1978, 1986 and 2022. The team has appeared in seven World Cup finals, including the first in 1930. It has won the [[Copa América]] a record 16 times, most recently in 2024. [[Lionel Messi|Messi]] has the most appearances for the team, with 208, and has scored the most goals, with 126.

Chemical element with symbol Ar and atomic number 18, a [[Noble gas|noble gas]] in group 18 of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. Argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere, at 0.934% (9340 ppmv), and the most abundant noble gas in the [[Earth's crust|crust]], at 0.00015%. Its name derives from the [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greek]] word for "lazy" or "inactive," reflecting its almost complete lack of chemical reactions. Argon forms no confirmed stable compounds at room temperature. [[Henry Cavendish]] suspected in 1785 that an unreactive gas was a component of air, and Lord Rayleigh and Sir William Ramsay first isolated argon from air in 1894. It is extracted industrially by fractional distillation of liquid air and is mostly used as an inert shielding gas in welding. It is also used in incandescent and fluorescent lighting, and it makes a distinctive blue-green gas laser.

Set of one or more premises directed toward a logical conclusion. An argument gives reasons for a conclusion through justification, explanation or persuasion. It can be studied from three perspectives: the logical, the [[Dialectic|dialectical]] and the [[Rhetoric|rhetorical]]. In [[Logic|logic]], an argument is a group of [[Proposition|propositions]], one of which is claimed to follow from the others through deductively valid [[Inference|inferences]]. In a valid argument the premises necessitate the conclusion, and a sound argument is one with true premises. Inductive arguments vary in strength: the stronger the argument, the greater the probability that its conclusion is true. In dialectics, an argument resolves a conflict of opinion between parties, while in rhetoric it is also judged by an audience in its context.

Self-contained piece for one voice, with or without [[Orchestra|orchestral]] accompaniment, normally part of a larger work. The typical context is [[Opera|opera]], but arias also appear in oratorios and cantatas, or as stand-alone concert pieces. The term originally meant any expressive [[Melody|melody]], usually sung. By the late 17th century, operatic arias took two main forms: binary (A–B) and ternary, or da capo (A–B–A), in which the opening section was repeated, often with decoration. Da capo arias with ritornelli, recurring instrumental episodes, became a typifying feature of European opera throughout the 18th century. Arias convey emotional content, in contrast to the speech-like recitative that carries the story line.

American singer, songwriter and actress. Known for a four-octave vocal range that extends into the whistle register, she began her career in the Broadway musical *13* and gained prominence as Cat Valentine in the [[Nickelodeon]] series *Victorious*. Her debut album, *Yours Truly* (2013), debuted atop the Billboard 200. She has amassed seven Billboard 200 number-one albums and ten Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles. She received an Academy Award nomination for portraying Glinda in *Wicked* (2024). She has won three [[Grammy Awards]] and is among the highest-certified artists in the United States.

Christological doctrine traditionally attributed to [[Arius]], a presbyter of [[Alexandria]]. It holds that the Son is distinct from the Father and subordinate to him, and was created by him. Historians including Rowan Williams, R.P.C. Hanson and Lewis Ayres argue that the term is a misleading label, since no single Arian party existed. Those who opposed the [[First Council of Nicaea|First Council of Nicaea]] and the [[Nicene Creed]] formed a loose coalition, united by opposition to *homoousios*. The doctrine is regarded as heretical by most mainstream Christian denominations and is held by a minority of modern groups, including [[Jehovah's Witnesses]].

Israeli general and politician, prime minister of Israel (2001–06). Born in Kfar Malal in Mandatory Palestine, he rose through the [[Israel Defense Forces|Israeli Army]] and became a noted field commander. As defense minister he directed the 1982 Lebanon War; an official inquiry found him personally responsible for ignoring the danger of bloodshed before the Sabra and Shatila massacre, and he was removed from the post. As prime minister he oversaw construction of the [[West Bank|West Bank]] barrier and the 2005 unilateral disengagement from the [[Gaza Strip|Gaza Strip]]. After a stroke in January 2006 he remained in a permanent vegetative state. Most Israelis revere him as a war hero and statesman, whereas Palestinians and Human Rights Watch have criticized him as a war criminal.

Ancient Greek comic playwright from [[Athens|Athens]]. He wrote forty plays, of which eleven survive virtually complete, most in the genre of Old Comedy, considered its most valuable examples. His plays were performed at the City Dionysia and the Lenaia, and several won first prize. He caricatured real figures including [[Euripides|Euripides]] and [[Alcibiades|Alcibiades]], and contemporary events such as the [[Peloponnesian War|Peloponnesian War]]. [[Plato|Plato]] singled out *The Clouds* as slander that contributed to the trial of [[Socrates|Socrates]]. His plays are marked by preposterous premises, explicit language, wordplay and political satire. He is known as the "Father of Comedy."

Greek business magnate and shipping tycoon. Born in Smyrna in the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman Empire]], he fled with his family to Greece in 1922 after the burning of Smyrna. He moved to Argentina in 1923 and became a tobacco trader and later a shipowner, amassing the world's largest privately owned shipping fleet. In Monaco he fought Prince Rainier III for economic control of the country through the Monte Carlo Casino. He had a long affair with opera singer [[Maria Callas|Maria Callas]], and in his final years was married to Jacqueline Kennedy, the former First Lady of the United States.

Cyrenaic presbyter and ascetic, central figure in the Arian controversy. Arius held that [[Jesus|Jesus]] Christ was not coeternal with God the Father but was created by God before anything else, a view of radical subordinationism. His dispute with Bishop Alexander of [[Alexandria|Alexandria]] catalyzed an existing doctrinal crisis. His teaching was condemned at the [[First Council of Nicaea|First Council of Nicaea]] in favor of homoousian conceptions of God and Jesus, and the [[Nicene Creed|Nicene Creed]] is described as a deliberately anti-Arian document. Modern scholars, including Rowan Williams, R.P.C. Hanson and Lewis Ayres, regard Arius as a conservative presbyter who gave voice to a broader theological trajectory rather than the founder of a sect. The label "Arianism" emerged largely from the polemics of [[Athanasius of Alexandria|Athanasius]]. Arian churches persisted for centuries in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa before being suppressed between the fifth and seventh centuries.

Landlocked state in the Southwestern United States, sharing the Four Corners region with Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. Its capital and largest city is Phoenix. It became the 48th state on February 14, 1912. Historically part of [[New Spain|New Spain]], it became part of independent Mexico in 1821, and Mexico ceded much of the territory to the United States after the [[Mexican–American War|Mexican–American War]] in 1848. The southernmost portion was acquired in 1853 through the Gadsden Purchase. The state contains the [[Grand Canyon|Grand Canyon]], and about one-quarter of its land is Indian reservations, including the [[Navajo Nation|Navajo Nation]], the largest in the state and the country.

Sacred storage chest and relic of the [[Israelites|Israelites]]. According to the Book of Exodus, it was a gold-plated acacia chest that held the Tablets of the Law, by which God delivered the [[Ten Commandments|Ten Commandments]] to [[Moses|Moses]]. Its fate is uncertain: Jewish traditions suggest it was taken to [[Babylon|Babylon]] or hidden, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church asserts it is housed in Axum. No verified evidence conclusively confirms its location today. Scholars debate the history of the Ark narratives in the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew Bible]] and possible Bedouin or Egyptian influences.

Landlocked state in the West South Central region of the Southern United States. It became the 25th state on June 15, 1836, after being part of the [[Louisiana Purchase|Louisiana Purchase]]. In 1861 it seceded and joined the [[Confederate States of America|Confederacy]], returning to the Union in 1868. Much of the Delta was developed for cotton plantations that depended on enslaved labor. During the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]], Little Rock was a major battleground for school integration. In the 1960s the state became the base of [[Walmart|Walmart]], headquartered in Bentonville. Its economy is based on services, aircraft, poultry, steel and tourism, with cotton, soybeans and rice as important crops.

Class of guided-missile destroyers of the United States Navy. Centered on the Aegis Combat System and the SPY-1D multifunction radar, the class was developed as a more affordable supplement to the Ticonderoga-class cruisers. Its multimission ships conduct antiaircraft warfare with [[Surface-to-air missile|surface-to-air missiles]], land strikes with Tomahawk missiles, and antisubmarine warfare with [[Sonar|sonar]]. As of April 2026, 75 ships were active and 24 more were planned, making it the most numerous class of [[Warship|warships]] in the U.S. Navy. It is named after Arleigh Burke, a destroyer admiral in [[World War II]] who later became Chief of Naval Operations, and it has the longest production run of any U.S. Navy surface combatant.

Upper part of the limb, between the shoulder and elbow joints, in strict anatomical usage. The forearm lies between the elbow and the wrist, and the [[Hand|hand]] lies beyond. The humerus is one of the three long bones of the arm and forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna. The arm's [[Skeletal muscle|muscles]] lie in two compartments separated by fascia. The anterior compartment holds the biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis, all supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve; the posterior compartment contains only the triceps brachii, supplied by the radial nerve. The brachial artery continues from the axillary artery. The radial nerve lies alongside the deep artery of the arm in a groove of the humerus, so a fracture of the bone's shaft can damage it. The [[Latin|Latin]] term *brachium* may refer to the upper arm as a whole or to the upper arm alone.
